Probability inequality

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 8k Articles: 86
Probability inequalities bound event probabilities from limited information, such as moments, without requiring a complete probability distribution. Markov's inequality uses a nonnegative random variable's expected value; Chebyshev's inequality uses a variance to bound deviations from a mean. The attraction is a guarantee that applies to many possible probability distributions. Their bounds can be conservative for a particular model, and distributions attaining equality show when the available information really cannot give more.

Lyapunov moment inequality (∥Z∥r​≤∥Z∥s​(0<r<s))

Words: 349
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
The Lyapunov moment inequality says that higher positive absolute moments give no smaller absolute moment sizes on a probability space. For a real random variable Z and 0<r<s,
(E∣Z∣r)1/r≤(E∣Z∣s)1/s,​
(1)
allowing an infinite value. For r≥1 the left expression is an Lp norm; below one it is a quasi-norm, so the usual triangle inequality terminology needs that distinction. The comparison uses a probability measure of total mass one; arbitrary unnormalized measure spaces need a factor depending on their total mass.
For a nonnegative count, the first moment size is its expected value, while the second is the square root of its second moment. Both ten-trial counts in second moment method have first moment size one. The independent count has second moment size 1.9​≈1.37840, whereas the shared-outcome count N=10B has second moment size 10​≈3.16228. The second moment distinguishes models with the same average because its square increases the influence of rare large counts.
More generally, for N=10B with a Bernoulli random variable B of parameter 1/10,
(ENr)1/r=10(1/10)1/r.
(2)
It rises from one at r=1 toward ten as r→∞. Replacing 1/10 by a parameter 0<q≤1 gives 10q1/r, which decreases toward zero for a fixed positive exponent when q↓0, making the rare-event and large-exponent limits different questions. For a scaled Rademacher random variable taking values −2 and two with equal probabilities, every absolute moment size is exactly two: increasing the exponent does not distinguish signs when the absolute value is constant.
For finite E∣Z∣s, apply the reversed Jensen's inequality to the strictly concave function tr/s and the nonnegative random variable ∣Z∣s:
E∣Z∣r≤(E∣Z∣s)r/s.
(3)
Taking the positive rth root proves the claim. Equality in this finite case holds exactly when ∣Z∣ is constant almost surely. If the higher moment is infinite, the upper bound is infinite and remains valid. Exponent zero is excluded from the statement; logarithmic or geometric limiting summaries require separately stated conventions, especially when Z can vanish.

Chebyshev's inequality (P(∣X−EX∣≥a)≤Var(X)/a2)

Words: 924 Articles: 3
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
For a real random variable X with finite variance σ2, expected value μ, and a threshold a>0, Chebyshev's inequality gives
P(∣X−μ∣≥a)≤a2σ2​.
(4)
One can also cap this upper bound at one, since a probability cannot exceed one. If σ>0, taking a=kσ gives P(∣X−μ∣≥kσ)≤1/k2. For example, at least 3/4 of the probability lies strictly within two standard deviations of the mean. This statement needs only the finite variance assumption. If the variance is zero, X=μ almost surely and every positive deviation threshold has zero tail probability.
Consider a random variable uniformly distributed on {−2,−1,0,1,2}. Its expected value is zero and its variance is (4+1+0+1+4)/5=2. At a=2 the actual tail probability is 2/5, while Chebyshev's inequality gives 2/22=1/2. At a=3 the actual tail probability is zero, while the bound is 2/9. A valid bound need not describe the exact shape or bounded support of a particular probability distribution.
For the standard normal distribution, the actual tail probabilities beyond two and three standard deviations are approximately 0.0455003 and 0.0026998, whereas the general bounds are 1/4 and 1/9. More knowledge of the probability distribution can therefore improve the estimate. The comparison does not diminish the guarantee: the three-point example in equality in Chebyshev's inequality attains it exactly.
The proof is a one-line use of Markov's inequality on the nonnegative random variable Y=(X−μ)2. The event ∣X−μ∣≥a equals Y≥a2, and EY=σ2. This explains why the denominator is squared and why a finite variance supplies the necessary information. [ref].
One important use is control of a sample mean. For independent and identically distributed random variables with finite variance σ2, the variance of a sample mean is σ2/n. Hence
P(∣Xn​−μ∣≥ε)≤nε2σ2​,ε>0.
(5)
For every fixed tolerance, the bound tends to zero as the sample size grows, proving the finite-variance case of the weak law of large numbers. For σ2=1 and ε=0.1, n=2000 makes the bound 0.05. This is a sufficient bound under the stated assumptions, rather than an optimal required sample size.
An early historical source is Pafnuty Chebyshev's 1867 paper “Des valeurs moyennes”, published in French translation by N. de Khanikof. Its opening theorem bounds deviations of sums using their expected values and second moments, linking averages with control of exceptional outcomes. [ref].

Equality in Chebyshev's inequality (P(X=μ−a)=P(X=μ+a)=σ2/(2a2))

Words: 67
Chebyshev's inequality OurBigBook.com
For a≥σ>0, assign probability σ2/(2a2) to each of μ−a and μ+a, and the remaining probability 1−σ2/a2 to μ. This probability distribution has expected value μ, variance σ2, and tail probability P(∣X−μ∣≥a)=σ2/a2. Thus Chebyshev's inequality is sharp when only these two moments are supplied. For example, μ=0, σ=1, a=2 gives masses 1/8, 3/4, 1/8. Replacing ≥ with > would exclude the two extreme points in this example.

Cantelli inequality (P(X−EX≥a)≤σ2/(σ2+a2))

Words: 447 Articles: 1
Chebyshev's inequality OurBigBook.com
Cantelli's inequality uses a mean and variance to control deviations in one specified direction. For a real random variable X with expected value μ, finite variance σ2, and a>0,
P(X−μ≥a)≤σ2+a2σ2​.​
(6)
Applying the same statement to −X gives the lower tail probability bound P(X−μ≤−a)≤σ2/(σ2+a2). No independence or particular probability distribution is required. If σ2=0, the random variable equals μ almost surely and both positive-threshold tail probabilities are zero.
For variance one and a threshold two above the mean, the upper-tail probability is at most 1/5. Applying the two-sided Chebyshev's inequality to contain that upper event would give the weaker bound 1/4. For the standard normal distribution, the actual upper tail probability at two is about 0.0227501, much smaller than either bound. Yet the two-point probability distribution in equality in Cantelli's inequality attains 1/5, showing why the smaller Gaussian value cannot be promised from these two moments alone.
A short explanation is to centre Y=X−μ and choose a nonnegative shift b. On Y≥a, the square (Y+b)2 is at least (a+b)2, so Markov's inequality gives
P(Y≥a)≤(a+b)2E(Y+b)2​=(a+b)2σ2+b2​.
(7)
The best shift is b=σ2/a, giving the displayed bound. Choosing the shift before squaring exploits the direction of the deviation; squaring the unshifted random variable treats both directions together. This shifted-square proof is also the strategy requested in the University of Utah's 2005 qualifying problem on Cantelli's inequality. [ref].
The one-sided improvement should be used for a one-sided question. Adding upper and lower bounds by the union bound gives 2σ2/(σ2+a2) for ∣X−μ∣≥a. When a≥σ>0, that is at least the Chebyshev's inequality bound σ2/a2; when a<σ, both two-sided expressions exceed one and must be capped. The separate one-sided bounds generally cannot be attained simultaneously by the same probability distribution.

Equality in Cantelli's inequality (P(X=μ+a)=σ2/(σ2+a2))

Words: 118
Cantelli inequality OurBigBook.com
For a>0 and σ2>0, place probabilities
P(X=μ+a)=σ2+a2σ2​,P(X=μ−aσ2​)=σ2+a2a2​.
(8)
Their weighted deviations cancel, giving expected value μ; their weighted squared deviations give variance σ2. Only the upper point belongs to X−μ≥a, so its tail probability attains Cantelli's inequality. With a=2, σ2=1, μ=0, the locations are two and −1/2, with masses 1/5 and 4/5. The optimized shift makes the lower point zero before squaring, explaining equality in the Markov's inequality step.
The threshold convention matters: this example has P(X−μ>a)=0. For a strict threshold, placing the upper point at a+ε instead gives probabilities approaching the same bound as ε↓0, with the prescribed mean and variance retained. Extra restrictions on the support of a probability distribution can change which extremal models are allowed.

First moment method

Words: 69
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
The first moment method uses the expected value of a count to control whether any counted occurrence exists. For a random variable N taking nonnegative integer values, Markov's inequality gives
P(N≥1)≤EN.
(9)
Consequently, EN<1 implies P(N=0)≥1−EN>0, proving that an outcome with no counted occurrence exists. For a sequence of such counts, EN→0 shows that N=0 with probability tending to one. The first moment method uses information about the average count, while the complementary second moment method also uses its variance.

Second moment method

Words: 463 Articles: 1
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
The second moment method uses a random variable's expected value and second moment to establish that a counted or measured quantity is positive with substantial probability. It is useful when a positive average alone could be caused by extremely large values on very rare outcomes. Controlling the variance rules out too much of that concentration in rare outcomes.
For a nonnegative random variable N with m=EN>0 and finite second moment, the second-moment bound for positivity gives
P(N>0)≥EN2(EN)2​=m2+Var(N)m2​.​
(10)
Equivalently, P(N=0)≤Var(N)/(m2+Var(N)). The method also includes the simpler Chebyshev's inequality bound P(N=0)≤Var(N)/m2. Thus a sequence of such random variables with Var(N)/(EN)2→0 has N>0 with probability tending to one. These statements require no independence assumption. The variance argument and its use for random counts are developed in Zhao's lecture notes. [ref].
For an original toy count, let N count successes in ten independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p=1/10. The binomial distribution gives
EN=1,Var(N)=9/10,EN2=19/10.
(11)
Consequently P(N>0)≥10/19≈0.526316. The exact probability is 1−(9/10)10≈0.651322. The first moment method and union bound only give the upper bound P(N>0)≤min{1,EN}=1 here. First and second moments therefore answer complementary existence questions.
For a sum of indicator random variables, the variance of a sum is
Var(∑i​Ii​)=∑i​Var(Ii​)+2∑i<j​Cov(Ii​,Ij​).
(12)
Independence makes the covariances vanish, but the formula itself also covers dependent counts. For the same ten success probabilities, let every trial share a single Bernoulli random variable B: then N=10B, with mean one, variance nine, and P(N>0)=1/10. The second-moment lower bound is exactly 1/10. Ignoring the positive covariances would produce the false independent-count conclusion. Zhao's discussion of sums of indicators explains why overlapping counted structures require these pairwise terms. [ref].

Second-moment bound for positivity (P(N>0)≥(EN)2/EN2)

Words: 125
Second moment method OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative random variable N with positive expected value and finite second moment, write N=N1{N>0}​. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
(EN)2=(E[N1{N>0}​])2≤EN2P(N>0),
(13)
which proves the bound in second moment method. It is the zero-threshold case of the Paley-Zygmund inequality. Equality occurs when N is a fixed positive value on the event N>0 and zero elsewhere, almost surely. For N=10B with B a Bernoulli random variable of parameter 1/10, (EN)2/EN2=1/10 equals the exact positivity probability.
The variance identity EN2=(EN)2+Var(N) turns the lower bound into a statement about variance relative to the squared mean. A small ratio forces positivity to be likely. A positive expected value alone does not do so: keeping EN=1 while taking N=1/q with probability q and zero otherwise makes the positivity probability as small as any chosen q>0.

Markov's inequality (P(Y≥a)≤EY/a)

Words: 507 Articles: 2
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative random variable Y and threshold a>0, Markov's inequality gives
P(Y≥a)≤aEY​.
(14)
The useful case has finite expected value; an infinite right side gives no finite information. The bound also holds if Y is nonnegative almost surely. Combining it with the elementary bound one gives P(Y≥a)≤min{1,EY/a}. Nonnegativity is essential: negative values could otherwise cancel the contribution of large positive values to the expected value.
The idea is an average budget. Every outcome where Y≥a contributes at least a times its probability to EY, and the other outcomes contribute nonnegative amounts. Formally, the indicator function gives Y≥a1{Y≥a}​; taking the expected value proves the bound. [ref].
For example, let Y take 0, 1, 2, 5 with respective probabilities 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. Its expected value is 1.1. At a=2, the tail probability is 0.3, while the bound is 1.1/2=0.55. At a=5, the tail probability is 0.1, while the bound is 0.22. A different probability distribution with the same expected value, putting masses 0.78 and 0.22 at 0 and 5, attains the bound 0.22 exactly at a=5.
Markov's inequality is useful when a moment is easy to compute but a full probability distribution is difficult to determine. A nonnegative count with expected value less than one must have some positive probability of being zero, giving the first moment method. Applying the same bound to a squared centered random variable gives Chebyshev's inequality. Applying it to an exponential function of a random variable gives an exponential Markov bound, which can exploit more than a single moment.

Equality in Markov's inequality (Y∈{0,a}almost surely)

Words: 60
Markov's inequality OurBigBook.com
For a finite-expected value nonnegative random variable and a>0, equality in the uncapped Markov's inequality holds exactly when Y takes only 0 and a almost surely. Indeed the nonnegative difference Y−a1{Y≥a}​ has zero expected value exactly when it vanishes almost surely. Giving a probability p yields EY=pa and P(Y≥a)=p. This shows the bound cannot generally be reduced using only the nonnegative random variable's expected value.

Exponential Markov bound

Words: 137
Markov's inequality OurBigBook.com
Applying Markov's inequality to the positive random variable etX gives
Pr(X≥x)≤e−txMX​(t),t>0.
(15)
Here MX​(t)=E[etX] is the moment-generating function, and the useful bound requires it to be finite at the chosen t. Optimizing over t>0 gives the Chernoff bound method: an exponential function weights large values more strongly before applying the same average-budget argument.
For example, let N have the Poisson distribution with parameter one. Its expected value and variance are both one, and its moment-generating function is MN​(t)=exp(et−1). At threshold four, choosing t=log4 gives
P(N≥4)≤exp(3−4log4)=256e3​≈0.0784591.
(16)
This t minimizes the exponent et−1−4t because its derivative is et−4, with positive second derivative. The direct Markov's inequality bound is 1/4, and the two-sided Chebyshev's inequality bound, applied to a deviation of at least three from the mean one, is 1/9. The exact Poisson distribution tail probability is 1−e−1(1+1+1/2+1/6)≈0.0189882. These compare three valid bounds obtained from progressively different information; none is an exact tail probability formula for general random variables.

A concentration inequality bounds the probability that a random variable differs substantially from a typical value such as its expected value or median.

Concentration of Lipschitz functions on the symmetric group (P(∣f−Ef∣≥t)≤2exp(−t2/(2nK2)))

Words: 111
Concentration inequality OurBigBook.com
Equip the symmetric group Sn​ with its uniform probability measure and unnormalized Hamming distance. If f has Lipschitz constant K, it obeys the displayed two-sided bound, and each one-sided tail has the same exponential without the factor two. Reveal a uniform permutation one image at a time. Two possible next images have completion sets paired by swapping those two values, changing exactly two coordinates. Thus the corresponding conditional means differ by at most 2K. Each increment of the Doob exposure martingale has conditional range length at most 2K. Applying the conditional Hoeffding lemma gives Eeλ(f−Ef)≤enλ2K2/2; optimizing the exponential Markov bound proves the bound. A mere absolute-increment bound of 2K gives a weaker constant, so using the range length matters.

Talagrand convex distance (dT​(x,A))

Words: 241 Articles: 3
Concentration inequality OurBigBook.com
For an event A in a product of finitely many probability spaces with its product measure, take the closed convex hull of the mismatch vectors (1xi​=yi​​)i​, y∈A. The distance of this hull from zero is dT​(x,A). Equivalently it is the supremum, over nonnegative coordinate weights of squared sum at most one, of their minimum mismatch sum. Averaging mismatch patterns is the feature that distinguishes this quantity from ordinary Hamming distance.

Their squared norm is at most λd12​+(1−λ)d22​+(1−λ)2. Hölder's inequality and induction bound that section's exponential integral by a−1infλ​r−λe(1−λ)2/4. Hoeffding inequality (P(Sn​≥t)≤e−2t2/V)

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Concentration inequality OurBigBook.com
The Hoeffding inequality turns finite interval bounds and independence into exponentially small tail probabilities for a sum. It requires neither a normal distribution nor identical probability distributions. Let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent essentially bounded real random variables, with deterministic finite bounds ai​≤Xi​≤bi​ almost surely. Define the centered sum and its squared-width budget by
Sn​=∑i=1n​(Xi​−EXi​),V=∑i=1n​(bi​−ai​)2.
(20)
For V>0 and t>0,
P(Sn​≥t)≤e−2t2/V,P(Sn​≤−t)≤e−2t2/V.​
(21)
The union bound therefore gives P(∣Sn​∣≥t)≤min{1,2e−2t2/V}. If V=0, every Xi​ is constant almost surely, so Sn​=0 and both positive-threshold tail probabilities vanish. The equal-width version is stated in the authored Stanford notes.[ref]
The quantity V is a sum of squared interval widths, not the variance of Sn​. Centering changes the endpoints to ai​−EXi​ and bi​−EXi​, leaving each width unchanged. For example, independent random variables in [−2,1] and [4,5] have V=32+12=10, whatever their expected values or probability distributions. A deviation at least three above their total expected value has probability at most e−18/10≈0.165299. If all widths equal b−a>0, the sample mean Xn​=n−1∑i​Xi​ satisfies
P(∣Xn​−EXn​∣≥ε)≤min{1,2exp(−2nε2/(b−a)2)},ε>0.
(22)
Independence is essential to this general guarantee. Take one Bernoulli random variable B with success probability 1/2 and set every Xi​=B. Each lies in [0,1], but for every n the sample mean is either zero or one. Thus P(∣Xn​−1/2∣≥1/4)=1, whereas incorrectly inserting these dependent observations into the formula would give 2e−n/8, less than one for n≥6. Some special dependent models have their own valid concentration inequalities; arbitrary statistical dependence cannot be ignored.
For the short proof, apply Markov's inequality to eλSn​ with λ>0, factor the expectation using independence, and apply the Hoeffding lemma to each factor:
P(Sn​≥t)≤e−λt∏i​Eeλ(Xi​−EXi​)≤exp(−λt+λ2V/8).
(23)
Minimizing this quadratic polynomial at λ=4t/V gives the upper tail probability; applying it to −Sn​ gives the lower one. This is the Chernoff bound method. The original 1963 article is Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables by Wassily Hoeffding; its publisher record identifies the article, but its full text was unavailable during this source check. The argument above is a direct derivation rather than a claim to have inspected that article's proof.

Hoeffding sample size for Bernoulli frequencies (n≥⌈log(2/δ)/(2ε2)⌉)

Words: 284
Hoeffding inequality OurBigBook.com
Let B1​,…,Bn​ be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with success probability p, and let p​n​=n−1∑i​Bi​ be their observed frequency, a sample mean. Since every interval width is one, V=n. Substituting t=nε into the Hoeffding inequality gives
P(p​n​−p≥ε)≤e−2nε2,P(∣p​n​−p∣≥ε)≤min{1,2e−2nε2}.
(24)
For tolerance 0<ε<1 and failure probability 0<δ<1, solving 2e−2nε2≤δ yields the sufficient sample size
n≥⌈2ε2log(2/δ)​⌉.​
(25)
Here log is the natural logarithm. For ε=0.05 and δ=0.05, n=738 guarantees an error smaller than 0.05 with probability at least 0.95, for every p∈[0,1]. The two-sided bound at this sample size is approximately 0.0499440. A specified single direction instead needs n≥⌈log(1/δ)/(2ε2)⌉, or 600 for these choices. Halving the tolerance multiplies the unrounded sufficient sample size by four; reducing the failure probability tenfold adds log(10)/(2ε2) before rounding.
This is a conservative sufficient sample size, not a necessary minimum. For a specified p, the count K=∑i​Bi​ has a binomial distribution, whose exact upper tail probability is
P(K≥k)=∑j=kn​(jn​)pj(1−p)n−j,k∈{0,…,n}.
(26)
For k>np, the Hoeffding inequality bounds this by exp[−2(k−np)2/n]. An arbitrary frequency threshold uses k=⌈n(p+ε)⌉; if k>n, the event is impossible. The discreteness of the count and its variance np(1−p) can make the exact tail probability substantially smaller. At n=100, p=1/2, k=60, the exact upper tail probability is about 0.0284440, while the bound is e−2≈0.135335. At p=1/10, k=20, the same deviation ε=0.1 gives the same bound but an exact upper tail probability about 0.00197856.

Hoeffding confidence interval (rn​=log(2/δ)/(2n)​)

Words: 133
Hoeffding inequality OurBigBook.com
For a fixed positive sample size n of independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables, let
rn​=2nlog(2/δ)​​,Cn​=[max{0,p​n​−rn​},min{1,p​n​+rn​}].

The Hoeffding inequality makes Cn​ a conservative confidence interval for p: Pp​(p∈Cn​)≥1−δ for every p∈[0,1]. Indeed, exclusion from the closed interval implies ∣p​n​−p∣>rn​, an event contained in the deviation event bounded by δ. Clipping to [0,1] retains coverage because p already lies there. For n=738, δ=0.05, and an observed frequency 369/738=1/2, rn​≈0.0499924, giving approximately [0.450008,0.549992].
Coverage concerns repeated independent samples: the unknown p is fixed and the confidence interval is random. This fixed-n guarantee does not justify repeatedly checking the same bound and stopping as soon as it looks favorable. The Hoeffding sample size for Bernoulli frequencies chooses n in advance; guarantees across repeated inspection times require separate control of the additional events, for example through a union bound with an allocated failure probability at each time.

A short proof exposes why the constant is 1/8. Put Y=X−EX and define exponential tilting by
dPλ​=eλY−ψ(λ)dP.
(30)
The tilted probability measure has the same interval of possible values, and differentiating the cumulant-generating function gives ψ′′(λ)=VarPλ​​(Y). Boundedness justifies these derivatives for every finite λ. Under any such tilted law, Popoviciu's inequality on variances gives ψ′′(λ)≤(b−a)2/4: the variance is no larger than the expected value of the squared distance from the interval midpoint, itself at most (b−a)2/4. This expression handles either sign of λ without changing the argument.

Efron–Stein inequality (Var(Z)≤21​∑i​E(Z−Zi′​)2)

Words: 748 Articles: 1
Concentration inequality OurBigBook.com
The Efron–Stein inequality bounds the variance of a complicated output by the effect of replacing one input at a time. Let X1​,…,Xn​ be mutually independent random variables, not necessarily identically distributed, and Z=f(X1​,…,Xn​) for a measurable function f, with EZ2<∞. Take X1′​,…,Xn′​ with Xi′​ having the same probability distribution as Xi​, all 2n inputs mutually independent. Define
Zi′​=f(X1​,…,Xi−1​,Xi′​,Xi+1​,…,Xn​).
(45)
Use the same function f, keeping every other input fixed. Then
Var(Z)≤21​i=1∑n​E[(Z−Zi′​)2].​
(46)
The expected value averages over both the original inputs and their replacements. An infinite right side gives a trivial bound; under the stated square-integrable condition every term is finite.[ref]
For a concrete four-state example, take independent Bernoulli random variables with P(X1​=1)=0.3 and P(X2​=1)=0.6, and set Z=max{X1​,X2​}. This output records whether either input is one. The states (0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1) have respective probabilities 0.28,0.12,0.42,0.18, so
P(Z=1)=0.72,Var(Z)=0.72(1−0.72)=0.2016.
(47)
Replacing X1​ changes Z only when X2​=0 and X1′​=X1​. A fresh Bernoulli draw can repeat the old value: the replacement is not a forced flip. By independence, the expected value of the squared change is
E[(Z−Z1′​)2]=0.4[0.7(0.3)+0.3(0.7)]=0.168.
(48)
Similarly,
E[(Z−Z2′​)2]=0.7[0.4(0.6)+0.6(0.4)]=0.336.
(49)
Thus Efron–Stein inequality gives 0.2016≤(0.168+0.336)/2=0.252. The larger second contribution reflects both its replacement probability and how often the other input leaves the output sensitive to it.
For the same inputs, consider instead W=X1​+2X2​. The variance of a sum of independent random variables gives
Var(W)=0.3(0.7)+4(0.6)(0.4)=1.17.
(50)
Here E[(W−W1′​)2]=0.42 and E[(W−W2′​)2]=1.92, so the Efron–Stein inequality is exact: (0.42+1.92)/2=1.17. More generally, for W=c+∑i​gi​(Xi​) with square-integrable summands, each contribution 21​E[(W−Wi′​)2] equals Var(gi​(Xi​)) and these variances add exactly.
Independence is essential. Let X1​=X2​=B for a single Bernoulli random variable with parameter 1/2, and take W=X1​+X2​=2B. Its variance is one. If each coordinate is nevertheless replaced by an independent draw from its marginal Bernoulli distribution, each squared-change expected value is 1/2, giving the false proposed upper bound 1/2. Replacement now creates off-diagonal states (0,1) and (1,0) that the original input never visits. The original coordinates fail the hypothesis of Efron–Stein inequality.
The attraction is local calculation: a function may involve many inputs, yet changing one can have a simple effect. Each half squared-change expected value supplies a coordinate's contribution to an upper budget for the total variance. Applying Chebyshev's inequality then bounds a tail probability using that budget. These contributions need not partition the actual variance, as the maximum example shows.
The name commemorates Bradley Efron and Charles M. Stein. Their 1981 paper The Jackknife Estimate of Variance appeared in The Annals of Statistics, volume 9, issue 3, pp. 586–596.[ref]

Boole's inequality (P(⋃i​Ai​)≤min{1,∑i​P(Ai​)})

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
Boole's inequality, also called the union bound, bounds the probability that at least one of several events occurs by adding their individual probabilities. For a finite or countable family of events Ai​ in the same probability space,
P(⋃i​Ai​)≤min{1,∑i​P(Ai​)}.
(60)
The union includes outcomes where several events occur together. There is no independence assumption: adding the individual probabilities counts such outcomes repeatedly, which can only make the sum larger. The cap at one uses the total mass of a probability measure. For infinitely many events, the sum is a nonnegative series, possibly infinite; an infinite sum gives only the bound one. This is countable subadditivity of a measure specialized to a probability measure. See Probability: Theory and Examples (fifth edition) by Rick Durrett (Section 1.1, Theorem 1.1.1(ii), printed p. 2).
For example, choose uniformly from the twelve outcomes Ω={1,…,12}, using the discrete uniform distribution. Put A={1,2,3,4}. If B={5,6,7,8}, these are disjoint events and their union has probability 8/12=2/3, exactly the union bound. If B={3,4,5,6}, the union has only six outcomes, so its exact probability is 1/2, although both individual probabilities are still 1/3 and the bound is still 2/3. If B=A, the exact probability falls to 1/3 with the same bound. These examples isolate overlap in the union bound by keeping the individual probabilities fixed.
The union bound is useful when each event is easy to control but their joint behavior is difficult to determine. A short proof uses indicator functions: at every outcome,
1⋃i=1n​Ai​​≤∑i=1n​1Ai​​.
(61)
Taking expected values and using linearity of expectation proves the finite bound.[ref] For a countable family, the finite unions increase to the full union; continuity of probability passes the finite inequalities to the limit. The closure of a sigma-algebra under countable unions ensures that this limiting union is an event. For the continuity of probability step, see Probability: Theory and Examples (fifth edition) by Rick Durrett (Section 1.1, Theorem 1.1.1(iii), printed p. 2).

Equality in Boole's inequality (P(Ai​∩Aj​)=0(i=j))

Words: 168
Boole's inequality OurBigBook.com
For finitely many events, or a countable family with finite sum of individual probabilities, equality in the uncapped union bound holds exactly when every pairwise intersection has probability zero. Equivalently, at most one event occurs almost surely. Pairwise disjoint events give equality, but literal disjointness is stronger than necessary: shared outcomes of probability zero do not change either side. For the capped bound, if the sum exceeds one, equality instead means that the union is an almost sure event; overlap can then have positive probability.
The cap and the disjoint case are both sharp. If the individual probabilities sum to at most one, put the events on separate pieces of a sample space to attain their sum. The twelve-outcome disjoint example does this with two events of probability 1/3. If the sum exceeds one, a covering union can attain the cap: on the same twelve-outcome sample space, A={1,…,8} and B={5,…,12} have sum 4/3 and exact union probability one. These are sharpness examples, not an assertion that every overlapping family attains the bound. Positive-probability disjoint events are also not independent events, because their joint probability is zero while the product of their individual probabilities is positive.

Overlap in the union bound (∑i​P(Ai​)−P(⋃i​Ai​)=E[N−1{N≥1}​])

Boole's inequality OurBigBook.com
For a finite family, the random variable N=∑i​1Ai​​ counts the events that occur. Linearity of expectation gives EN=∑i​P(Ai​), while P(N≥1) is the exact union probability. Their difference is
∑i​P(Ai​)−P(⋃i​Ai​)=E[N−1{N≥1}​].
(62)
An outcome in exactly k≥1 events contributes k−1 extra counts, weighted by its probability. This nonnegative difference vanishes exactly in equality in Boole's inequality. For two events it is P(A∩B), as the inclusion-exclusion principle for probabilities shows. For more events, the Bonferroni inequalities use pairwise and higher intersection information to bound the exact union probability; blindly subtracting pairwise intersections from the sum gives a lower bound, rather than a corrected upper bound.
Severe overlap can make the union bound arbitrarily pessimistic. Let all m events be the same event A with probability 1/m, where m≥1 is an integer. A concrete model is the discrete uniform distribution on {1,…,m} with A={1}. The exact union probability is 1/m, whereas the sum and capped bound are both one. The ratio is m: adding more names for the same event does not create more ways to fail. The identity above describes the gap in the uncapped sum; capping at one can reduce that gap.

Failure-probability budget (P(⋂i​Fic​)≥max{0,1−∑i​δi​})

Words: 342
Boole's inequality OurBigBook.com
A failure-probability budget assigns nonnegative numbers δi​ to a finite or countable family of failure events Fi​ in a common probability space, with verified bounds P(Fi​)≤δi​. The union bound guarantees that the probability of any failure is at most min{1,∑i​δi​}. By De Morgan's laws and the complement rule of probability, the probability that every requirement succeeds obeys
P(⋂i​Fic​)=1−P(⋃i​Fi​)≥max{0,1−∑i​δi​}.
(63)
Thus ∑i​δi​≤δ guarantees simultaneous success with probability at least 1−δ, even when all failure events depend on the same observations. The numbers δi​ are upper allowances; adding them is not a calculation of the exact failure probability.
For three requirements, give each a failure-probability budget δi​=1/20. The total budget is 3/20, so simultaneous success has probability at least 17/20. On a sample space of twenty equally likely outcomes, let F1​={1}, F2​={2}, and F3​={3}. These disjoint events attain the budget and the success bound. If instead all three failure events equal {1}, their individual probabilities are unchanged, but exact failure has probability 1/20 and simultaneous success has probability 19/20. This second model shows how overlap can leave the guarantee conservative.
For n requirements, an equal allocation δi​=δ/n is convenient; unequal allocations also work when some requirements are harder to satisfy. For infinitely many requirements indexed by i≥1, the allocation δi​=δ/2i uses total budget δ by the geometric series. A fixed positive allowance for every requirement instead gives an infinite sum and no positive simultaneous-success guarantee from the union bound. The individual probability bounds must cover all the failure events being combined: omitting possible failure modes leaves the resulting guarantee about the listed requirements only. The same addition of error allowances underlies the Bonferroni correction in simultaneous hypothesis tests.

Positive common intersection from pair-intersection probabilities (P(⋂i​Ai​)≥∑i<j​P(Ai​∩Aj​)−(2n​)+1)

Words: 47
Boole's inequality OurBigBook.com
For n≥2, the intersection of all pairwise intersections Ai​∩Aj​ is ⋂i​Ai​. Apply the union bound to the complements of the pairwise intersections and then take the complement to obtain the displayed lower bound. A sum exceeding (2n​)−1 therefore forces positive common probability without any independence assumption.

FKG inequality

Words: 383 Articles: 11
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
The FKG inequality gives positive association under a log-supermodular probability measure on a finite distributive lattice.

FKG lattice condition (P(ω∧η)P(ω∨η)≥P(ω)P(η))

Words: 101 Articles: 1
FKG inequality OurBigBook.com
This lattice condition on configuration masses is the hypothesis of the FKG inequality. A product measure on a finite Boolean lattice satisfies it with equality, since in each coordinate the minimum and maximum retain the original two coordinate values. It implies positive association of random variables for increasing functions.

Exponential-tilt proof of positive association

Words: 60
FKG lattice condition OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive law μ satisfying the FKG lattice condition on a finite Boolean lattice, and an increasing function g, tilt to μt​(ω)∝etg(ω)μ(ω). For t≥0, the lattice inequality and g(ω∨η)≥g(ω) give the Holley condition for μt​≥st​μ. For any increasing f, differentiate Eμt​​f≥Eμ​f at t=0 from the right. The derivative is Covμ​(f,g), proving positive association of random variables.

Words: 266 Articles: 8
FKG inequality OurBigBook.com
Increasing events under a product probability measure are positively associated: P(A∩B)≥P(A)P(B).

Square-root bound for increasing events (P(A)≥1−1−P(A∪B)​)

Words: 31
Harris-FKG inequality OurBigBook.com
For two increasing events of equal probability a under a product measure, positive association of their complements gives 1−P(A∪B)≥(1−a)2. Hence a≥1−1−P(A∪B)​. For r equal-probability increasing events, the same reasoning gives a≥1−(1−P(⋃j​Aj​))1/r.

Square-root trick for positively associated events

Words: 17
Harris-FKG inequality OurBigBook.com
If increasing events A1​,…,Ak​ have a common probability, applying the Harris-FKG inequality to their decreasing complements gives P(A1​)≥1−(1−P(⋃i​Ai​))1/k.

Harris' inequality

Words: 202 Articles: 5
Harris-FKG inequality OurBigBook.com
Harris' inequality states that two increasing events under an independent Bernoulli product measure are positively correlated.
Negative correlation of increasing and decreasing events (P(E∩G)≤P(E)P(G))
Words: 46
Harris' inequality OurBigBook.com
Under a product measure on a finite Boolean lattice, an increasing event E and a decreasing event G obey the displayed inequality. The complement Gc is an increasing event, so Harris' inequality gives P(E∩Gc)≥P(E)P(Gc). Subtract from P(E) to obtain the result. This implication includes degenerate Bernoulli distribution parameters 0 and 1.
Increasing event
Words: 140 Articles: 3
Harris' inequality OurBigBook.com
An event in a partially ordered configuration space is increasing when changing coordinates upward cannot make a configuration leave the event.
Sharp threshold
Words: 66
Increasing event OurBigBook.com
For a sequence of nontrivial increasing events on finite product measures, write px​ for the parameter at which the success probability is x. An additive sharp threshold means that p1−ε​−pε​→0 for every fixed 0<ε<1/2. When the threshold parameter itself tends to zero, relative sharpness instead compares this window with p1/2​; additive sharpness alone is then a weaker assertion. The Friedgut-Kalai sharp threshold theorem provides an explicit additive bound for transitive increasing events.
Transitive increasing event
Words: 37
Increasing event OurBigBook.com
An increasing event on a finite product of identically distributed coordinates is transitive if a group action preserving the event is transitive on the coordinate set. Its influences are all equal. Transitivity concerns coordinates, and does not assert transitivity on successful configurations.
Decreasing event
Words: 16
Increasing event OurBigBook.com
An event is decreasing when closing additional edges cannot destroy it. Its complement is an increasing event.

Janson inequality

Words: 163 Articles: 3
Probability inequality OurBigBook.com
For increasing containment events Ai​ in a Bernoulli product space, let X=∑i​1Ai​​, μ=EX, and
Δ=∑i=j:Ai​∼Aj​​P(Ai​∩Aj​),
(64)
where the sum is ordered and dependency means overlapping coordinate supports. Then
P(X=0)≤e−μ+Δ/2.
(65)
In particular it is at most e−μ/2 when Δ≤μ, and at most e−μ2/(2Δ) when Δ≥μ.

Janson lower-tail bound by independent thinning (Pr(X≤μ−a)≤exp[−a2/(2(μ+Δ))])

Words: 54
Janson inequality OurBigBook.com
For increasing containment indicators, attach independent Bernoulli selectors of parameter t. Janson inequality applied to the selected events gives E(1−t)X≤exp(−tμ+t2Δ/2). Set t=1−e−s and apply the exponential Markov bound. The estimates s−s2/2≤1−e−s≤s give exponent at most −sa+s2(μ+Δ)/2. Optimizing at s=a/(μ+Δ) proves the displayed lower-tail bound, with the dependency sum ordered and excluding the diagonal.

P(I1​=⋯=Im​=0)≤∏i​(1−EIi​+∑j<i:j∼i​E(Ii​Ij​)).
